implementation_notes: The pattern is syntax in C#: a method that returns Task or Task<TResult> starts the operation and hands back the handle, async turns the method body into a state machine that returns at the first incomplete await, and await is the collect step - suspending the caller instead of blocking its thread, then rethrowing the operation's exception at the await site. Task.WhenAll/WhenAny, ContinueWith and ValueTask are the composition and allocation-conscious forms, Task.Run moves CPU-bound work to the thread pool, and CancellationToken/IProgress<T> are the conventional parameters for the pattern's cancellation and notification concerns. Microsoft's own guidance is explicit that TAP supersedes the two legacy shapes: the APM Begin/End pair over IAsyncResult, and the EAP Async-suffix method with a Completed event.
pitfalls: async void cannot be awaited, so exceptions propagate to the captured SynchronizationContext and completion cannot be tracked; return Task or Task<T> and, for intentional fire-and-forget, give the returned task to an explicit owner or error sink.
Blocking on a task (.Result, .Wait()) inside a synchronization context (UI, legacy ASP.NET) deadlocks, because the continuation needs the thread that is blocked; await all the way down instead.

Adding async does not offload CPU work: the state machine runs synchronously until the first incomplete await, so long CPU work before it still blocks the caller; use Task.Run or a dedicated scheduler only when explicit offloading is intended.

An abandoned task's exception is not rethrown at the abandoning call site; it may surface later through TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException and is not a reliable handling path, so retain and observe the task or route it to an explicit error sink.

variants.name: Classic APM: BeginOperationName / EndOperationName over IAsyncResult
variants.implementation_notes: The hand-written ancestor of TAP: each long-running operation gets a BeginOperationName that starts it and returns an IAsyncResult handle (with IsCompleted, AsyncWaitHandle, AsyncState and a caller-supplied AsyncCallback) and an EndOperationName that blocks until completion and returns the result or throws the operation's exception. The two-call shape separates invocation from collection explicitly and remains the contract of many older framework APIs (FileStream.BeginRead/EndRead, WebRequest.BeginGetResponse), which is why implementations still have to recognise it - the current bridge is Task.Factory.FromAsync, which adapts the Begin/End pair into a Task. Keep the shape only for legacy interfaces, never for new API design.
pitfalls: Every BeginOperationName must be matched by exactly one EndOperationName: ending twice, or ending with an IAsyncResult from another operation, is undefined and leaks or misreports the result.
The callback runs on a thread-pool thread and typically calls EndOperationName there, so its thread affinity differs from the caller - shared state must be synchronised.
Exceptions thrown by BeginOperationName before the operation starts are thrown to the caller, all later ones only from EndOperationName - easy to swallow if End is never called.
Forgetting to end the operation leaks the IAsyncResult's wait handle; the pattern has no using/await sugar to make that impossible.
